# Adenopathy(Archived)

**Authors:** Ruby Maini, Shivaraj Nagalli

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

The lymphatic system is a complex component of the immune system that plays a crucial role in filtering substances throughout the body. Lymphocytes are the integral agents involved in searching for target proteins and travel through lymph nodes, which are diffusely placed throughout the body. Lymphadenopathy refers to the swelling of lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small glands that are responsible for filtering fluid from the lymphatic system. They are divided into sections known as follicles, which are further subdivided into B zones and T zones, representing the base location of lymphocytic maturation. Abnormal proliferation of lymphocytes may be a result of inflammation, infection, or malignancy; therefore, clinicians must perform a detailed history and physical examination to screen for lymphadenopathy. When inspecting for lymphadenopathy, one should carefully examine all pertinent anatomic regions, including the neck, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions. In general, the size of a normal lymph node in the adult population should be less than 1 cm; however, there are exceptions to this rule.
